I want to like this game, but there are some frustrating design flaws that detract from what should be a fun hacklite game. I kept running into the same issues time and again throughout the campaign, here are a couple of examples.

- There are some storylines that require you to play perfectly to proceed. Failure can lock you out from retrying, and many times the way forward is very obtuse. For example, in one mission you must stop an assassin from boarding a train. To unmask the assassin in the first place you must have played efficiently enough in previous missions, to have had enough spare time left to investigate several non-objective data nodes. Then you have to figure out that one of the terms in an email can be searched for on the In[T]ranet, and then recall information from over a dozen missions earlier. In this mission you must now disrupt the track to delay the train, without affecting any other tracks, which also means failure. First you have to be inquisitive enough (and have enough trace time to) investigate a non-objective data node and find out that the target train has been rescheduled from track C to Track B. Upon sabotaging track B you get an update showing that the objective to stop the assassin from boarding was successful! Mission complete right? Well apparently not. Disconnecting at this stage gives you a blank mission summary and prevents you from reattempting the mission. As much as I want to know what went wrong I'm not willing to start the game from the beginning to try and find out.

- The RNG can really mess you up. This one is pretty simple, you need to use a stealth program to avoid the trace bar filling up. Instead of being based on turns or measured progress, it's a % chance to increase every turn. This means that sometimes running restrictive heavy stealth can fail you several times in a row, or sometimes token measures will prevent a trace for many turns in a row. Some missions have very low trace bars, meaning a bit of bad RNG can cause you to fail. Running into (randomly placed) ICE also increases trace, and you are forced to either waste time scanning for it or run into it headlong. There are many other examples of RNG messing up your timing or causing undue grief.

- The game throws a lot of unexpected curveballs and suckerpunches at you. This is made worse by the fact that you can only carry (by default) 5 programs with you on each mission.  Sure the portscanner on the mission selection screen will generally give you broad sense of what you might be facing, but the specifics really do matter. What if you pick hive (an attack program that is very weak at the start of the mission but becomes more powerful as you infect more nodes) and a wall ICE spawns between the access node and the rest of the network? Suddenly you spend half the trace bar just breaking through the first obstacle, leaving no time for the mission objectives. There's also a poorly pre-informed boss battle where the boss ICE/AI may randomly destroy one of your software packages. Yes, you can hack a specific node to disable this attack, but RNG decided that he would use it immediately on me and remove my only breaker app (ie I'm now unarmed against a boss). The game really likes throwing these kinds of scenarios at you out of left field, and failure usually means you can't re-attempt the mission without starting a new game.

- The Morality Penalty. Simply put, blackhat actions reward you grossly while whitehat actions leave you starving for resources. In many cases the whitehat missions available have no payout or even ask you to spend credits on the mission itself. Some of the better attack programs are also locked behind blackhat rank, while whitehat will give you an extra defensive option or two (sitting still spamming defensive measures is not great, a lot of missions have timers).

All in all, many of these could have been alleviated if there wasn't such a reliance on RNG or bringing the perfect combination of apps. As it is, many missions feel more like a gamble than proper foresight or strategy.

review_text_raw:
Midnight Protocol is rich in ambience, in intrigue, in tangled relationships of regret and camaraderie confidently conveyed in nothing more than text, and in more than its fair share of ingenuity.

It's also, unfortunately, like playing chess with only five pieces against a kid who can, at any time, go "yeah no but I had this super power set up HERE, right, all along I had this set up I did, and that means you can't get my guy and, uh, and, um, and and and WHOOOAAA EARTHQUAKE FLIPPED THE BOOOOARD"

You, master hacker that you are, are allowed to do two - count 'em - two succulent and juicy things per turn, and have to sulkily type out 'end' to end your turn thereafter. The goal is to make the most of limited resources against a seemingly unassailable adversary through deft moves and cunning. So far, so hacking-mentality - applaudable.

Yet the execution just doesn't quite make it. Effective red-teaming is about having recon good to go in advance against your target, which you never have in Midnight Protocol - and which costs you precious scant actions per turn to execute in the field instead. The jaws close on you all the while, unless you turn off the Trace mechanic altogether in the game options, and then you're just left with slowly hopping two-by-two across the board poking at things and slowly slurping up cash.

The plot is compelling, rich in injustices and laced with what-ifs, and I wanted to push through and see more of it. Unfortunately, there's a fair bit of padding in the early game that killed the momentum for me. I get it's good to establish characters, lay down rules and playstyles etc., but it'd be so much more exciting for these tidbits to come through organically while enjoying unravelling the story.

A shame, as there's a lot of cool-factor to the whole affair - it just isn't that fun to play.

The randomness that governs the trace mechanic makes the puzzles more frustrating than fun to solve when using stealth strategies.

UI decisions make collating the information the puzzles give you very difficult (e.g. to guess a password from a data node, first you have to open the data command, memorize your guess, close the data command, then input your guess).  Similarly, email conversations aren't viewable in mission.

The core seems like it could be fun, but the frustrations detract too much.

Stopped having fun after 2 hours and do not intend to continue :( Game seems okay but I could not figure out which tools to use correctly to finish levels. You can cheat the system by keep restarting but I do not find that approach fun. I try to do my best first try every level and roll with the punches but like I said I could not figure out a good way to do it. 

You can bring 5 tools with you to every level, and there is a trace counter increasing at every step where the maximum trace results in a failure. Then you need to bring an item called cloak to decrease the probability of gaining trace, then because you need to use cloak you cannot use some other items so they are gone. If there are blockers in your way you need the sniffer to find them and dagger to destroy them while hoping cloak does its work. This is already 3 out of 5 items fixed for you. I don't know, I do not get it and I do not find it fun so I do not recommend the game.

[url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/beatnuki/recommended/1162700/]I pretty much gotta agree with this review[/url].

The developers advertised it on Netrunner adjacent boards. Unfortunately, that's as far as the Netrunner elements go.

You're playing a computer hacker (aka: "Runner" which isn't the term here, so not Netrunner releated) breaking into systems to figure out what has gone on since you were released from jail. Mayhem and hacking ensues.

But the thing is: For all the talk about being Netrunner inspired... it doesn't work. Both you and the AI/SysOp have two actions a turn (compared to Netrunners' 4 Runner 3 SysOp actions a turn). This would be fine... [b][i]IF[/i] the gameplay wasn't timed with the "trace" mechanic[/b] (unlike Netrunners, you can't remove it and you can't buy over the SysOp/Corp to bounce it/avoid the trace).

So you're racing against the clock, facecheck (slam into an ICE defense) and... get fucked over massively in terms of the timer/trace raising in addition to losing an action to where you can't course correct same turn. This means you'll get "trace++" 2+ traces in addition to the end turn trace (which if some ICE is hit, turns off your "cloak" function to try to prevent/stop the trace from increasing, say HELLO to 2-3+ traces off a faceslam).

[i]This is where the game becomes unfun[/i] and if I didn't run into the above review, I would've quit instead of finding the "turn the trace mechanic off" and as the review states: That makes the game somewhat boring because you're [i]turning off an anxiety/timer mechanic[/i] but after a certain point you're like "ok, I'm screwed five ways, why have a sixth?"

Interesting story to go through, but honestly: No, not worth the money. Check the demo out, if you're able to put up with the bad design (needed some more passes to be a bit more fair on the players), go for it. But honestly? I can't recommend it.

Hopefully NetSpectre gives me the Netrunner-a-like I want, but I'm kind of doubting it.

Slay the Spire is pretty much the only one that comes close and even THAT isn't going for Netrunner, but took elements from it.

...My search continues...

review_text_raw: A hacking strategy game where there are a lot of interesting decisions to create an aesthetic and a feeling that I'm sure someone who isn't me would love. Basically the way the game works is you select the different programs (abilities) you want and enter a map. You are being traced so a timer is constantly counting down (though there are ways to mitigate this) and you have two actions each round. You move around the system, trying to find your goal (money or data), evading and neutralizing security countermeasures and dealing with other challenges, before the trace gets back to you and you have to exit the system. My main issue is that the aesthetic decision of making the gameplay all done command line style, so you're typing "move a0" to move to a node instead of clicking or managing the memory allocated to one of your programs by typing "slice cloak 2". It slows down the pace of the game and makes it repetitive and laborious. The strategy gameplay itself is interesting if a bit swingy from RNGy and somewhat oppressive from the fact that you only get one chance on any mission. The negatives just build up to make it feel tedious and frustrating.
